title: 9 AI Techniques You Probably Haven't Tried
dek: A personalized cancer vaccine clears phase III and reignites the fight over what counts as 'AI' — then NLW switches into operator mode with nine techniques, from live voice mode to team agents to local Qwen, that even power users probably haven't tried yet.

oneIdea.headline: AI is changing faster than your habits — nine techniques to catch up before fall.
oneIdea.summary: The thing that makes AI exciting is the thing that makes it hard: it changes constantly, and even power users settle into comfortable workflows while the frontier moves on. With back-to-school season approaching, this episode aggregates what people are learning in public — live voice mode, teaching agents by letting them watch, writing skills, /design, multiplayer AI, GrokBot, local models, and two-word prompts — as a menu for your next experimental day.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: The melanoma vaccine result is the one thing here a patient may actually raise with you
items.body: Moderna and Merck's personalised mRNA vaccine extended remission in a phase III trial of more than 1,100 patients with advanced melanoma, and lung cancer trials are running. Two practical points for the surgery. First, the mechanism is worth being able to explain in a sentence: the tumour is sequenced, its mutations identified, and an mRNA vaccine made to that individual's cancer — it is adjuvant to existing immunotherapy, not a replacement for it, and not a preventive vaccine in the sense patients will assume. Second, it is not available here, and a phase III readout is the start of a regulatory and manufacturing road, not the end of one. The honest answer to 'should I be asking for this?' is that it is genuinely encouraging, that it applies to a specific advanced-melanoma population under specialist care, and that any route to it now is through their oncology team or a trial. Worth reading the eventual paper rather than the press release.

items.title: Ambient voice is the next scribe question — 'let the AI watch you work' is not
items.body: Two of the nine techniques matter to a practice that already uses a scribe, and they pull in opposite directions. Ambient voice mode — speaking to the assistant continuously rather than clicking to dictate — is a plausible extension of what a scribe already does, and if a supplier offers it the governance questions are the familiar ones: what is recorded between consultations, when does the microphone stop, and can a patient decline it as easily as they can decline the scribe. The other technique, letting the tool keep a timeline of your screen activity and turn it into repeatable processes, is a straightforward no on a clinical desktop. A general-purpose product logging what is on a GP's screen is logging identifiable patient data into a consumer service with no DPIA, no data processing agreement and no lawful basis. It is a good idea in a marketing department and an information governance incident in a consulting room.

items.title: If Zitron's right, don't let the workflow live only in the tool
items.body: NLW's framing is that habits should be rebuilt every few months around whatever is newest. Zitron's counter-argument this week is that the company underwriting several of these tools may not be able to pay its bills, and that users could be moved onto other providers or lose the free tier. Both readings point to the same practical discipline for a practice. If a way of working is worth adopting — a letter-writing standard encoded as a reusable instruction, a triage summary format, a coding prompt — write it down somewhere the practice owns, as plain text, so it can be moved to another vendor in an afternoon. That costs nothing if NLW is right and saves the winter if Zitron is. The same applies to the scribe: know what the fallback is before you need it, because the answer 'we go back to typing' is only tolerable if someone has checked the appointment book can absorb it.

the_other_side.text: Nothing newer had been published, so the counter-source is Monday's essay again — but the half of it that bites on a nine-techniques menu is a different half. Most of the tools on this list sit on one company that, by Zitron's arithmetic, carries over $800bn of compute commitments through 2030, needs $100–200bn a year in fresh capital, and lost $20.9bn on $13.07bn of revenue in 2025; his conclusion is that "at some point, OpenAI will simply not be able to pay its bills". What he sketches for users rather than investors is customers handed "API keys that flow to Microsoft AI Foundry", the free ChatGPT tier stripped back, and no further training of the models people had built their week around. He is not arguing that voice mode or computer history fail to work — he is arguing the entity underwriting them may not be there to keep them working.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is durability: whether tools you build habits on this autumn still exist, at the same price and capability, in two years. Both accept the features work now and that the firms shipping them lose money at scale. The empirical question that resolves is whether OpenAI closes its next raise, and the observable that settles it is the terms — a round at or above the $852bn mark by roughly March 2027, versus a down round, a Microsoft absorption, or a quiet rescue. The residue is worldview: Whittemore treats capability as the thing that compounds and financing as someone else's problem; Zitron treats financing as what determines whether capability survives. Whittemore is vindicated if the money arrives and these techniques become ordinary; Zitron if a funding failure strands them. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: none of this is yet paid for by the people using it. Watch the next raise, and its price.

headlines.headline: The thing that will work is actually curing cancer.
headlines.attribution: Dario Amodei, responding to critics of his messaging
headlines.summary: Responding to critics of his negative messaging, the Anthropic CEO argued that no glitzy marketing campaign wins back public trust — 'saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliché than it is inspiring.' A day later, a lot of people were saying that's exactly what had happened.

headlines.headline: A personalized cancer vaccine clears its first late-stage trial
headlines.summary: Moderna and Merck's treatment analyzes cancerous cells, identifies the DNA mutation, and creates a personalized mRNA vaccine — extending remission in more than 1,100 advanced melanoma patients in a successful phase III trial, with lung cancer trials underway. Mass General's Dr. Ryan Sullivan: 'these approaches may change the way we treat cancer more broadly.'

headlines.headline: Call it machine learning if you want — just don't dismiss it
headlines.summary: Critics are right that this isn't scientists plugging results into ChatGPT — it's advanced ML closer to AlphaFold, and the brilliant human scientists shouldn't be erased by attributing the breakthrough to 'AI.' But it would also be dismissive to call it hype: the AI era's investment in compute, research, and talent fed this, and the market noticed — Moderna jumped 70%, then 125%, within hours.

headlines.headline: OpenAI's private safety processing ends the monitoring-vs-privacy trade-off
headlines.summary: For eligible API customers with zero-data-retention agreements, fully automated, encrypted scanning now covers entire agentic sessions — no human ever sees sensitive data, and flagged issues reach staff only as anonymized category-and-severity summaries. OpenAI's Adam GPT: 'This is one of those small things that is actually a huge thing' — and per NLW's enterprise conversations, that's absolutely true.

headlines.headline: Anthropic's Fable shows the cost of getting this wrong
headlines.summary: Anthropic's answer to long-horizon agent safety was to simply disable zero data retention for Fable and scan full session data — a complete non-starter for many enterprise customers, showing up in fairly dismal enterprise adoption. OpenAI's new approach is aimed squarely at that gap.

headlines.headline: Replit's 'free mode' runs everything through GPT 5.6 Luna
headlines.summary: Not literally free — $20/month subscribers can use Replit without burning usage credits, with all queries routed through Luna for a claimed 30× more output, and escalation to stronger models still available for complex tasks. Replit: 'AI models are now capable and affordable enough to make once unreachable outcomes practical.'

headlines.headline: OpenAI is fighting on two frontiers at once
headlines.summary: They're competing at the state of the art with 5.6 Sol and the Astra model to come — but since Luna launched, they're also clearly looking behind them at the Chinese open-weight models and refusing to surrender that ground. As users mature in matching power levels to tasks, expect much more competition on the efficiency frontier, not just the capability frontier.

headlines.headline: SpaceX-Cognition deal talk: everyone can be telling the truth
headlines.summary: Bloomberg reported SpaceX approached the coding-agent startup — which raised at $26B in May and is seeking $40B+ — before CEO Scott Wu shot it down ('Cognition is not for sale and we haven't been talking') and Elon backed him. NLW's read: 'approaching someone about a deal' is blurry enough that nobody needs to be lying — that shoulder-nudge conversation is genuinely how these offers start, and Elon's appetite for app-layer acquisitions wasn't sated by the Cursor deal.

headlines.headline: The White House safety framework is a black box — even to the labs
headlines.summary: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google staff were handed paper copies at the closed-door unveiling and allowed only to take notes; written versions still haven't been distributed. Cato's Juan Ladano: 'a framework that raises more questions than the one it answers is worse than no framework at all' — and especially in light of the week's data-center trust discussions, NLW fully agrees.

headlines.headline: The meta-technique: steal from people experimenting in public
headlines.summary: This episode isn't NLW's own testing — it's an aggregation of what others are sharing, because one of the things that makes AI so cool is that people learn in public. For as cesspool-y as they can be, if you're not watching the AI conversation on X and LinkedIn, you're missing a lot of free R&D.

headlines.headline: Live voice mode is the highest-vibe feature of the summer
headlines.summary: Dan Shipper says almost everyone at Every is 'freaking out' about voice mode in ChatGPT for work, and Allie K. Miller credits Codex voice mode for finishing all her urgent work at 2 AM — firing off thumbnail requests, doc retrieval, and email checks while she fills her water bottle. 'Holler if you need me' is now a prompt.

headlines.headline: It's not a use case — it's ambient interaction
headlines.summary: Miller's point: ambient assistant versus click-to-speak 'probably sounds like a negligible difference... but it is a world of distance in practice' — less a chief of staff than 'an ambient workforce, an ambient voice-controlled operating system.' NLW's advice: you won't get it from descriptions; commit to a period of working this way, even if it feels weird at first.

headlines.headline: Stop explaining your workflow — let the AI watch it
headlines.summary: ChatGPT's computer history keeps an ambient timeline of how you actually work and turns it into repeatable processes, while GrokBot takes the deliberate approach: press a button and it watches a specific task as you do it. If you'd written something off as too hard to explain to AI, that may have changed significantly.

headlines.headline: Turn the AI-writing tell list into a permanent skill
headlines.summary: Instead of endlessly prompting 'rewrite without the tropes' — the tiny dramatic sentences, 'it's not this, it's that,' the AI clapping for itself — print Ruben Haseed's post of dead giveaways as a PDF, drop it into Claude, and make it a skill so it never happens again. Others are converting full style guides, like the ASD-STE-100 standard for plane manuals, the same way.

headlines.headline: Claude Code's /design command fixes iteration at both macro and micro
headlines.summary: The new artboard interface lets you preview a batch of templates and give high-level feedback when you don't yet know what you want — and then highlight and edit specific regions rather than re-prompting the whole design. In NLW's experience, it improves the design loop at both ends.

headlines.headline: Agent skills are a discipline, not a binary
headlines.summary: Matt Pocock's repository groups skills by when you'd actually use them — getting started, main flow, shaping, upkeep — each with a copyable install. His 'Grill with Docs' skill interviews you about a plan until you and the agent 'share one understanding of it,' writing the vocabulary and hard decisions into your repo as a leave-behind.

headlines.headline: Multiplayer AI is going to be the big trend of the fall
headlines.summary: Since Open Claw, we've run agents in single-player mode — personal chiefs of staff and research agents working for one person. But work is collaborative, full of handoffs and shared context, and the big opportunity is agentic tools that live where teams intersect rather than where individuals work alone.

headlines.headline: Claude Tag makes the agent a teammate, not a tool
headlines.summary: Unlike the older tag-to-summon Slack integration, Claude Tag joins a channel as a team member with the entire channel's context — with permissions, tool access, and context that can differ channel by channel. Crucially, that Claude is a shared resource across the team, not something living on one person's computer.

headlines.headline: The Citizen SDLC: from personal prototype to company production
headlines.summary: 10x, an AI build partner out of New York, published a six-stage lifecycle that takes what non-technical employees vibe-code with AI from a personal prototype to production the whole company can use — another attack on the same problem of individual AI wins never scaling to the team.

headlines.headline: A week in, GrokBot users are still finding the ceiling
headlines.summary: Its own virtual computer solves the access issues that plagued earlier agents, and X is full of use cases — application reviews, sales deck updates, Salesforce reports, daily briefings — plus patterns like a chief-of-staff bot managing all the others. Lenny Rachitsky suggests pointing it at an MCP of his 500+ podcast transcripts as a personal product-strategy advisor; for the Grok-averse, Nous Research's new Hermes Desktop bot mode is the open, more controllable alternative.

headlines.headline: Local AI just got a real reason to try again: Qwen 3.8 27B
headlines.summary: The model runs on common hardware and scores 52 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — a level that would have been state of the art just a few months ago. If you've been meaning to experiment with local AI, this is the moment to dive in.

headlines.headline: Two-word prompts: 'Now what?' 'Please fix.' 'Simulate it.'
headlines.summary: Allie K. Miller's 18 two-word prompts read like talking to a teammate: 'Now what?' when you've finished a push and want more; 'Please fix' with a screenshot; 'Simulate it' to run scenarios and edge cases; 'Remember this' to force the AI to log a mistake in memory rather than hoping it does so automatically. Not a workflow overhaul — just simple ways to get more from tools you already use daily.
